summary: store{8,16}_lane decodes incorrectly without the memory64 feature
description:
### Summary

When wasmi is built with `simd` but without `memory64`, some `v128.store8_lane` and `v128.store16_lane` instructions seem to be decoded wrong. In debug builds this panics; in release builds I got wrong results and sometimes a crash. Default builds have `memory64` and look fine.

### Details

I think the decoder reads the `offset` of these instructions as a `u64`, while the encoder writes it as `Offset`, which is a `u32` without `memory64`:
https://github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi/blob/05d2de3057c323a3f807ef23eb19e0c2ab58d2a8/crates/ir/src/decode/op.rs#L270-L276

It happens when the vector comes from a local and the offset is 65536 or more, or the store goes to a memory other than 0. Changing the field to `pub offset: Offset` fixed it for me. I have a small patch with a test if that helps.

### Proof of concept

wasmi 2.0.2 with `default-features = false, features = ["std", "validate", "simd"]`:

(module
  (memory (export "memory") 2)
  (func (export "_start") (local v128)
    (local.set 0 (v128.const i32x4 0x11223344 0x55667788 0x99aabbcc 0xddeeff00))
    i32.const 0
    local.get 0
    v128.store8_lane offset=65536 3))

After `_start`, memory[65536] should be 0x11.
- Debug: panic, "failed to decode `OpCode` ... invalid bit pattern".
- Release: a MemoryOutOfBounds trap, and memory is not written.

Some fuzzer modules (attached) crash with SIGSEGV in release. With `memory64` on, all of them work as in Wasmtime.


### Impact

Builds of wasmi 2.0.0-beta.4 to 2.0.2 with `simd` and without `memory64`. A module can crash the host or get wrong results. I am not sure whether it can do more.

### Summary

A use-after-free vulnerability has been discovered in the linear memory implementation of Wasmi. This issue can be triggered by a WebAssembly module under certain memory growth conditions, potentially leading to memory corruption, information disclosure, or code execution.

### Impact

- **Confidentiality:** High – attacker-controlled memory reads possible.
- **Integrity:** High – memory corruption may allow arbitrary writes.
- **Availability:** High – interpreter crashes possible.

### Affected Versions

Wasmi `v0.41.0` through Wasmi `v1.0.0`.

### Patches

The following versions have patches available that fix this bug:

1. Wasmi `v0.41.2`, `v0.41.3`
2. Wasmi `v0.47.1`, `v0.47.2`
3. Wasmi `v0.51.3`, `v0.51.4`, `v0.51.5`
4. Wasmi `v1.0.1` (and later)

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to the latest patched version of Wasmi.
- Consider limiting the maximum linear memory sizes where feasible.

### Credits

This vulnerability was discovered by **Robert T. Morris (RTM)**.

### References

`CVE-2025-66627`

summary: Out-of-bounds Write for host to Wasm calls with more than 128 Parameters
description:
### Summary

In the WASMI Interpreter, an [Out-of-bounds Buffer Write](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/787.html) will arise arise if the host calls or resumes a Wasm function with more parameters than the default limit (128), as it will surpass the stack value. This doesn’t affect calls from Wasm to Wasm, only from host to Wasm.

### Impact

After conducting an analysis of the dependent Polkadot systems of `wasmi`: [Pallet Contracts](https://github.com/paritytech/polkadot-sdk/tree/master/substrate/frame/contracts), [Parity Signer](https://github.com/paritytech/parity-signer), and [Smoldot](https://github.com/smol-dot/smoldot), we have found that none on those systems have been affected by the issue as they are calling host to Wasm function with a small limited amount of parameters always. 

### Mitigations

If you are using `wasmi` betwen version 0.15.0 and 0.31.0, please update it to the [0.31.1](https://github.com/paritytech/wasmi/releases/tag/v0.31.1) patch release that we just published.

### Workarounds

Ensure no more than 128 parameters can be pass in a call from the host to a Wasm function. 

### References

Patch PR: <PR>

### Special thanks

Special thanks to Stellar Development Foundation for reporting this security vulnerability.
